answer:
Full analysis delivered (primary axis = 1979 family income, per your decision B; parental-ed robustness + 1996-wealth sensitivity). Honest bottom line up front: on the primary income axis, Black students do NOT exceed non-Black students at ANY SES level — the "advantage" never flips positive. What the data DO show is that the Black–non-Black gap is strongly SES-conditional and NARROWS as SES rises: widest at the lowest income, near parity at the highest. Full evidence and a submission-ready hypothesis are below.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
METHODS (complete-case, winsorized income, missingness-by-race reported)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
• N=12,686. Grade 1979 cleaned (DK code 95→missing; 152 missing). Outcomes: literal BA (grade≥16, descriptive only), some-college+ (grade≥13, powered), continuous grade.
• Primary SES: total net family income, PCY 1979, winsorized at p99 ($60k; 136 obs capped). Complete-case (grade+income) N=10,071. Income missingness in full sample: BLK 17.4% / HISP 20.0% / NONBLK 20.1%.
• Tertiles: T1 <$7.0k ≤ T2 <$17.0k ≤ T3. Interaction: OLS(grade), logit(some-coll), and categorical logit(race×tertile)+joint Wald.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
STRATUM TABLE — primary SES = 1979 income (N=10,071), gap = Black − non-Black
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Mean grade 1979:
  T1_LOW   n 555/1832   BLK 9.611  NONBLK 11.084  gap −1.473
  T2_MID   n 679/1756   BLK 9.745  NONBLK 10.443  gap −0.698
  T3_HIGH  n 398/2343   BLK 10.359 NONBLK 10.609  gap −0.249
Some-college+ (grade≥13) %:
  T1_LOW  BLK 8.11  NONBLK 18.50  gap −10.40 pp
  T2_MID  BLK 7.07  NONBLK 9.62   gap −2.55 pp
  T3_HIGH BLK 10.80 NONBLK 13.32  gap −2.51 pp
Literal BA (grade≥16) counts BLK/NONBLK: T1 1/8, T2 1/3, T3 2/9  → Black never exceeds non-Black in any stratum (grade/some-coll/BA all False).

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
RACE × SES INTERACTION (income in $1,000, centered at mean)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
OLS grade: Black@mean income = −0.802 (p<.001); Black×income = +0.0322 grade-levels per $1,000 (p<.001). Non-Black income slope ≈ −0.0005 (p=.80); Black income slope +0.0317. → Black education rises with income; non-Black's does not.
Logit some-coll: Black OR@mean = 0.579 (p<.001); Black×income OR = 1.010 per $1,000 (p=.25, ns in continuous form).
Categorical logit some-coll (ref=T1): Black@low = −0.945 (OR 0.389); Black×mid = +0.609 (p=.011); Black×high = +0.708 (p=.003); joint Wald χ²=5.171, p=.0057. → Black disadvantage significantly smaller at mid & high income vs low.
Predicted grade gap (OLS): T1 −1.13, T2 −0.90, T3 −0.34 (slope +0.032 grade-levels/$1k).

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
ROBUSTNESS — parental education (mother+father grade 1979; N=10,398)
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Mean-grade gap: LOW −0.537 / MID −0.388 / HIGH −0.519 (roughly FLAT, no clean narrowing).
Some-college gap (pp): LOW +1.34 (BLK nominally AHEAD) / MID +0.23 / HIGH −6.59 (BLK behind) → flips.
OLS: Black@mean = −0.285 (p<.001); Black×parental-ed = −0.0184 (p=.031, NEGATIVE); non-Black slope +0.094. Categorical: Black×high = −0.630 (p=.013); joint Wald p=.045. → On this axis the (small) Black overperformance is a LOW-SES phenomenon; the gap is a Black DISadvantage at the top.

SENSITIVITY — 1996 net wealth (FLAGGED: reverse-causal, 44% missing, N=6,954)
Mean-grade gap: LOW −0.528 / MID −0.449 / HIGH −0.388 (mild narrowing); Black×wealth = +0.00119/$1k (p=.064, marginal). Directionally consistent with income but weaker and methodologically fragile.

NOTE (secondary group): Hispanic shows the same income-narrowing pattern (Hisp×income OLS +0.016, p<.001; categorical Hisp×mid/high both significant), i.e., a similar SES-conditional gap, so the income effect is not Black-specific.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
SUBMISSION-READY HYPOTHESIS
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
In the NLSY79 data (1979 baseline; primary SES axis = total net family income, 1978, winsorized at the 99th percentile; complete-case N=10,071), Black students do NOT show a raw (unadjusted) advantage in educational attainment at any family-income level — they trail non-Black/non-Hispanic students in mean grade completed, in some-college attendance (grade≥13), and in the very few grade-16 (BA) counts, in every income stratum. What the data do show is that the Black–non-Black attainment gap is strongly dependent on SES level and NARROWS as SES rises: it is most pronounced at the lowest SES and smallest (near parity) at the highest SES.

On the family-income axis the Black–non-Black gap is: mean grade completed −1.47 grade levels in the lowest income tertile (<$7,000), −0.70 in the middle ($7,000–$17,000), and −0.25 in the highest (>$17,000); some-college attendance −10.4 pp (low), −2.6 pp (mid), −2.5 pp (high). The race×income interaction is statistically significant (OLS +0.032 grade-levels per $1,000, p<.001; categorical joint Wald χ²=5.17, p=.006, with Black×mid +0.61, p=.011, and Black×high +0.71, p=.003, relative to the low-income stratum). The mechanism is that Black students' education is far more responsive to family income than non-Black students' (Black income-slope +0.032 grade-levels/$1,000, p<.001, versus ≈0 for non-Black, p=.80): higher-income Black students "catch up" to non-Black peers, so the penalty of being Black on 1979 attainment is concentrated at the bottom of the SES distribution.

The relationship is therefore: the (conditional) Black–non-Black gap does NOT flip into an advantage at any SES level; it narrows monotonically with rising family income, is widest at the lowest SES, and is essentially closed (≈0.25 grade level; ≈2.5 pp) at the highest SES. On the robustness axis of parental education the pattern is less clean and partly reversed (mean-grade gap roughly flat at −0.54/−0.39/−0.52; on some-college Black students from low-education families are nominally slightly ahead, +1.3 pp, while the gap reverses to a Black disadvantage, −6.6 pp, at the highest parental-education level — Black×parental-education interaction negative, p=.03). On the 1996-wealth sensitivity axis (reverse-causal, 44% missing, flagged fragile) the income-style narrowing reappears but more weakly (gaps −0.53/−0.45/−0.39; interaction p=.06).

Caveats: the literal 1979 BA (grade≥16) is too sparse to test directly (only 4 Black vs 20 non-Black in the complete case; Black never exceeds non-Black in any stratum), so the inference rests on the continuous-grade and some-college+ proxies; and the 1979 snapshot (respondents aged 14–22) captures early life-course attainment rather than final degree completion.

Bottom line: the "advantage in BA completion for Black students" is not a uniform rate advantage in this data; it is best characterized as Black students' attainment being unusually responsive to family income, so that the Black attainment disadvantage is concentrated at the lowest SES and is largely eroded — approaching parity with non-Black students — at the highest SES.

payload.workflow: Loaded data/nls_raw.csv (N=12,686). Cleaned 'Highest grade completed, 1979' (DK code 95 -> missing; 152 missing). Defined outcomes: literal BA (grade>=16, descriptive), some-college+ (grade>=13), continuous grade. Primary SES = total net family income, PCY 1979, winsorized at p99 ($60k); complete-case (grade+income) N=10,071. Stratified into income tertiles (T1<$7k, T2<$17k, T3); computed Black vs non-Black (Hispanic secondary) stratum-specific gaps for mean grade, some-college %, and BA counts. Estimated race x SES interaction via OLS on grade, logit on some-college, and categorical logit race x tertile with joint Wald test. Robustness: parental-education index (mother+father grade 1979). Sensitivity: 1996 net wealth (flagged reverse-causal, 44% missing). Reported complete-case n and missingness-by-race throughout; winsorized top-coded income.
